statements.text: The store with the highest revenue also has the largest staff.

explanation: Check each statement separately against the table, sorting or computing only the column it needs. Statement 1: Sort by revenue: Midtown is first with $745k. prompt: For each of the following statements, select True if the statement is true based on the information provided. Otherwise select False.

statements.text: The property with the highest gross yield (annual rent ÷ price) also has the highest net yield.
Every property built in 2000 or later has a higher net yield than every property built before 2000.
The total NOI of the three cheapest properties exceeds the NOI of Linden Sq and Willow Pl combined.

explanation: Check each statement separately against the table, sorting or computing only the column it needs. Statement 1: Gross yield: Spruce Dr 7.09% is highest, Aspen 7.05%. Net yield: Birch 4.59%, Aspen 4.62%, Spruce 4.45%. Spruce's 6 vacancy weeks pull its net yield below Aspen's and Birch's. The statement is False. Statement 2: Post-2000 lowest net yield: Linden Sq 4.21%. Pre-2000 highest: Aspen Way 4.62%. Aspen beats Linden. The statement is False. Statement 3: Cheapest three: Aspen (13.78k), Spruce (14.92k), Birch (16.75k), total ≈ 45.45k. Linden (24.42k) + Willow (20.22k) ≈ 44.63k. The statement is True.

title: Diagnostic lab audit
intro: An auditor sent known samples to six labs. Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN); specificity = true negatives ÷ all actual negatives, where actual negatives = samples - TP - FN; precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP).
prompt: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the condition described is met according to the information in the table. Otherwise select No.

statements.text: Lab F has the highest sensitivity of the six labs.
Every lab has a specificity above 97%.
The lab with the lowest precision also has the lowest testing cost per true positive found.

explanation: Check each statement separately against the table, sorting or computing only the column it needs. Statement 1: Sensitivity: F 264/273 ≈ 96.70%, C 505/517 ≈ 97.68%, A 95.81%. Lab C is highest. Answer: No. Statement 2: Lowest specificity is Lab C: negatives = 6,100 - 517 = 5583, (5,583 - 183)/5,583 ≈ 96.72%. All others are higher (Lab A 97.82%). Answer: No. Statement 3: Precision: C 73.4% is lowest. Cost per TP = samples × cost ÷ TP: C ≈ $423, A ≈ $530, E ≈ $492, F ≈ $588. C is lowest on cost too. Answer: Yes.

title: Trade profile of nine economies
intro: A trade bulletin summarizes 2024 goods trade. Export growth is the change from 2023. Commodity share is the percent of exports that are raw commodities.
prompt: For each of the following statements, select True if the statement is true based on the information provided. Otherwise select False.

statements.text: Among countries whose commodity share exceeds 50%, the one with the largest trade surplus as a percent of imports is Amaran.
Valoria added more dollars of exports from 2023 to 2024 than Yarrow, Amaran and Corim combined.
The dollar value of Westria's commodity exports is greater than the dollar value of Brisa's commodity exports.

explanation: Check each statement separately against the table, sorting or computing only the column it needs. Statement 1: Commodity share over 50%: Westria, Yarrow, Amaran, Corim. Exports ÷ imports: Amaran 1.116, Yarrow 1.052, Westria 0.793, Corim 0.880. Amaran is highest. The statement is True. Statement 2: Added = exports - exports/(1+g). Valoria ≈ 11.11bn. Yarrow ≈ 6.44, Amaran ≈ 6.29, Corim ≈ 5.61, sum ≈ 18.34bn. Valoria is lower. The statement is False. Statement 3: Westria: 96 × 0.63 ≈ 60.5bn. Brisa: 210 × 0.21 = 44.1bn. Westria is higher. The statement is True.

intro: The bar chart shows the quarterly revenue of a small kitchenware company in 2024.
text: Revenue was highest in [[1]], and Q4 revenue was [[2]] million dollars greater than Q1 revenue.

options: Q1
Q2
Q3
Q4

explanation: Read each bar. The tallest bar is Q4 at $6.3 million, so blank 1 is Q4. For blank 2, subtract the Q1 value from the Q4 value: 6.3 - 4.2 = 2.1, so Q4 was $2.1 million higher. Do not confuse the difference with Q4's own level of 6.3 or with the gap between neighbouring quarters such as Q4 - Q3 = 1.6.

intro: A travel blog tracked its monthly visitors for the first half of the year.
text: The largest month-over-month increase in visitors occurred in [[1]], and the blog had about [[2]] thousand visitors in May.

options: February
April
May
June

explanation: Compute each monthly change: Feb +5, Mar -2, Apr +13, May +3, Jun +5. The biggest jump, 13 thousand, is from March to April, so blank 1 is April. For blank 2 read the May point directly: 61 thousand visitors. A common slip is to pick June because it has the highest level, but the question asks about the largest increase, not the highest value.

intro: The chart shows the number of employees in each department of a mid-sized software firm.
text: The largest department has [[1]] times as many employees as the smallest, and [[2]] departments have more than 50 employees.
explanation: Both blanks depend on exact bar heights, so read each value from the axis first. The largest department is Engineering with 112 employees and the smallest is Legal with 14. Their ratio is 112 ÷ 14 = 8, so blank 1 is 8. For blank 2, count the bars above 50: Sales (64), Engineering (112) and Marketing (52). Support is 48, just below the line. That gives 3 departments. Watch the bars that sit close to the threshold.

chart.title: Units sold by region and product, March

intro: A consumer electronics retailer stacks its monthly unit sales by product line in each region.
text: Total units sold in the North region were [[1]] hundred, and in the South region the product line with the most units sold was [[2]].

options: Laptops
Tablets
Phones

explanation: For blank 1, add the North segments: 120 + 60 + 90 = 270 hundred units. For blank 2, compare the three segments of the South bar: Laptops 85, Tablets 95, Phones 70. Tablets is the largest segment, so blank 2 is Tablets. In a stacked chart, read each segment as the difference between its top and bottom edges rather than reading the top edge alone.

intro: The chart compares average daily high temperatures in an inland city and a coastal city in the same country.
text: The inland city was warmer than the coastal city in [[1]] of the eight months, and the largest gap between the two cities in any month was [[2]]°C.
explanation: Compare month by month. Inland minus coastal: Jan -5, Feb -4, Mar -2, Apr +1, May +2, Jun +3, Jul +4, Aug +2. The inland city is warmer in April through August, which is 5 months. The largest absolute gap is 5°C in January, when the coastal city is warmer. If you only look at months where inland is warmer, you get 4°C, which is the trap. Blank 2 is 5.

intro: Each point represents one store in a franchise network.
text: The relationship between ad spend and sales is [[1]], and the store that spent $18,000 on advertising had sales of about [[2]] thousand dollars.

options: strongly positive
weakly positive
close to zero
negative

explanation: The points rise steadily from lower left to upper right with little scatter around a straight line, so the relationship is strongly positive (the correlation coefficient is about 0.996). For blank 2, find x = 18 on the horizontal axis and read the point above it: about $101 thousand. Note that a positive association does not show that advertising caused the sales.

intro: A construction supplier tracks the average price it paid for a standard spool of copper wire.
text: From 2020 to 2024 the price rose by [[1]]%, and the average price over the five years was [[2]] dollars.
explanation: Blank 1 is a percent change, so the starting year is the base; blank 2 is a simple mean. Percent change = (new - old) ÷ old × 100 = (60 - 48) ÷ 48 × 100 = 25%. The trap is 20%, which uses 2024 as the base. For blank 2, add the five prices: 48 + 56 + 71 + 64 + 60 = 299, and divide by 5 to get $59.8. Even though the price peaked at 71 in 2022, it ended the period 25% above its starting level.

intro: The stacked bars show a country's electricity generation by source every two years.
text: In 2020, renewables supplied [[1]]% of total generation, and renewable generation in 2024 was about [[2]] times its 2016 level.
explanation: In a stacked chart, each segment is one source and the full bar is the total. In 2020 total generation is 40 + 31 + 21 + 8 = 100 TWh, so the renewable share is 21 ÷ 100 = 21%. Because the total happens to be 100, the segment height equals the percent. For blank 2, divide 2024 renewables by 2016 renewables: 34 ÷ 12 ≈ 2.83, about 2.8 times. Reading 34 - 12 = 22 as the answer confuses an absolute difference with a ratio.

intro: The chart shows a region's annual unemployment rate before and after an economic shock.
text: From 2019 to 2020 the unemployment rate rose by [[1]] percentage points, and from 2020 to 2024 it fell by about [[2]]%.
explanation: Rates expressed in percent can change in two different ways, and the blanks test both. A percentage-point change is a simple difference: 7.5 - 4.0 = 3.5 points. (The relative change, 87.5%, is the trap for blank 1.) For blank 2 the question asks for a percent change in the rate itself: (4.2 - 7.5) ÷ 7.5 × 100 ≈ -44%, a fall of about 44%. Subtracting 7.5 - 4.2 = 3.3 points and calling that 33% mixes the two ideas.

chart.title: First-year enrolment by program and gender

intro: A university reports first-year enrolment in five programs, split by gender.
text: The program with the largest gap between male and female enrolment is [[1]], and female students make up about [[2]]% of first-year enrolment across the five programs.

options: Business
Computing
History
Nursing

explanation: Read both bars for every program before comparing, since the gap is what matters for blank 1. Gaps: Biology 80, Business 20, Computing 270, History 20, Nursing 280. Nursing (340 vs 60) edges out Computing (420 vs 150), so blank 1 is Nursing. For blank 2, total female = 1200 and total male = 1110, a combined 2310. Female share = 1200 ÷ 2310 ≈ 51.9%, about 52%. Averaging the five program percentages would weight small programs too heavily.

intro: The chart shows the month-end share prices of two listed companies.
text: From January to June, Alder's share price rose by [[1]]% while Birchway's rose by 15%; Alder's largest one-month percent gain came in [[2]].

options: February
April
May
June

explanation: Percent change compares each move with its own starting price, so the cheaper share can win even with a smaller dollar gain. Alder: (50 - 40) ÷ 40 = 25%. Birchway: (138 - 120) ÷ 120 = 15%, so although Birchway gained more dollars (18 vs 10), Alder gained more in percent terms. For blank 2, monthly gains for Alder are Feb 10.0%, Mar -11.4%, Apr 23.1%, May 8.3%, Jun -3.8%. The April gain from 39 to 48 is the largest, about 23%.

intro: Each point shows one student in a test-prep class.
text: The scatter plot shows a [[1]] association between hours studied and score, and [[2]] students scored above 80 while studying fewer than 12 hours per week.

options: strong negative
moderate positive
perfect positive
no clear

explanation: Scores generally rise with hours but with plenty of spread (for example 6 hours gives 58 and 5 hours gives 72), so the association is positive but only moderate; the correlation is about 0.84. For blank 2, look left of 12 hours and above 80: the points at 7 hours (81) and 10 hours (84). The 12-hour point at 90 is not fewer than 12. So blank 2 is 2.

intro: A nonprofit's annual spending is stacked by category.
text: Programs accounted for about [[1]]% of total spending in 2024, and total spending grew by about [[2]]% from 2022 to 2024.
explanation: Shares and growth both require the full bar totals, so add the segments of each bar first, then divide; the Programs segment alone cannot answer either blank. 2024 total = 610 + 175 + 300 + 85 = 1170. Program share = 300 ÷ 1170 ≈ 25.6%, so about 25%. 2022 total = 540 + 180 + 210 + 70 = 1000. Growth = (1170 - 1000) ÷ 1000 ≈ 17.0%, about 17%. A tempting error is to report the growth of Programs alone (about 43%) or to compare segment heights without totals.

intro: The chart shows the age distribution of a mid-sized town of 100,000 people.
text: The median resident falls in the [[1]] age group, and residents aged 55 and over make up [[2]]% of the population.
explanation: For a median from grouped data, accumulate the groups from the youngest until you pass half the total. The total is 100 thousand, so the median is the 50th thousand resident counted from the youngest. Running totals: 17, 29, 43, 58. The 50th thousand falls in the 35-44 group. For blank 2, 55-64 has 12 thousand and 65+ has 17 thousand, so 29 thousand out of 100 thousand, which is 29%. Picking 17% counts only the 65+ group.

intro: A startup plots the cumulative number of downloads of its app at the end of each month since launch week.
text: From the end of January to the end of July the app averaged about [[1]] thousand new downloads per month, and the most new downloads in a single month occurred in [[2]].

options: March
May
June
July

explanation: A cumulative line never falls, so the useful information is in the size of each step up. On a cumulative chart, new downloads are the differences between points. Average monthly new downloads = (68 - 12) ÷ 6 = 9.3 thousand. Monthly new downloads are Feb 8, Mar 11, Apr 8, May 13, Jun 9, Jul 7, so the peak month is May. Choosing July because it has the highest cumulative total confuses the level with the change.

intro: The chart compares a country's annual goods exports and imports.
text: The trade deficit (imports minus exports) was largest in [[1]], and in 2024 exports covered about [[2]]% of imports.
explanation: The deficit is the vertical gap between the paired bars in each year, not the height of either bar, so compute it year by year. Deficits by year: 2019 12, 2020 4, 2021 16, 2022 23, 2023 11, 2024 7. The largest is 23 billion in 2022. Note that 2024 has the highest imports but a smaller gap. For blank 2, export coverage = 118 ÷ 125 × 100 = 94.4%, about 94%. The trap 106% inverts the ratio (imports ÷ exports).

chart.title: Ticket price vs. weekly tickets sold

intro: A cinema tested a different ticket price each week for eight weeks.
text: On average, each $1 increase in price reduced weekly tickets sold by about [[1]], and of the prices tested, weekly ticket revenue was highest at a price of [[2]] dollars.
explanation: Use the two end points to estimate the slope, then test revenue at each tested price. From $8 to $22 tickets fall from 940 to 410, a drop of 530 over $14, about 38 per dollar (the best-fit slope is -37.4). For blank 2, compute price × tickets: 12 × 800 = 9,600; 14 × 710 = 9,940; 16 × 650 = 10,400; 18 × 560 = 10,080; 20 × 500 = 10,000. The maximum, 10,400, occurs at $16. The lowest price sells the most tickets but does not maximize revenue.

intro: The stacked bars show the share of a national smartphone market held by three firms and all others. Each bar totals 100%.
text: Between 2021 and 2024, Firm C's share grew at an average compound rate of about [[1]]% per year, and by 2024 Firm C's share was [[2]] percentage points behind Firm B's.
explanation: Each bar totals 100%, so segment heights can be read directly as market shares. Firm C rose from 16% to 24%, a factor of 1.5 over three years. The compound annual rate r solves (1 + r)³ = 1.5, so r ≈ 14.5%, about 14%. Dividing the 50% total gain by 3 gives about 17%, which ignores compounding. For blank 2, in 2024 Firm B holds 34% and Firm C holds 24%, a gap of 10 percentage points.

intro: A logistics company plots annual revenue and operating cost. Operating profit = revenue - operating cost; margin = profit ÷ revenue.
text: The operating margin was highest in [[1]], and operating profit in 2024 was [[2]]% higher than in 2019.
explanation: First turn the two lines into a profit for each year. Margin is a ratio, so the year with the most profit is not necessarily the year with the best margin. Profits: 2019 8, 2020 5, 2021 11, 2022 11, 2023 14, 2024 14. Margins: 2021 19.0%, 2022 16.7%, 2023 19.4%, 2024 17.5%. The highest margin is 2023, even though 2024 has the highest revenue. Profit grew from 8 to 14, so (14 - 8) ÷ 8 = 75%. The trap 60% is the revenue growth over the same period.

chart.title: Income per person vs. life expectancy, 12 countries

intro: Each point represents one country in a regional health report.
text: Life expectancy shows a [[1]] relationship with income, and [[2]] of the countries with GDP per capita above $25,000 have a life expectancy below 80 years.

options: positive, flattening at higher incomes
positive and accelerating
negative
no clear

explanation: Look at the overall shape of the cloud first, then count only the points that satisfy both conditions. Life expectancy rises quickly from 61 to about 72 as income moves from 4 to 14, then gains only about 12 more years over the next $46 thousand, so the relationship is positive but flattening (diminishing returns). For blank 2, countries above 25 are at 28 (78), 33 (74), 39 (81), 45 (82), 52 (83) and 60 (84). Only 28 and 33 are below 80, so the count is 2.

intro: A streaming service reports year-end subscribers stacked by plan.
text: From 2022 to 2024 the plan whose share of total subscribers rose by the most percentage points was [[1]], and total subscribers grew by about [[2]]%.

options: Basic
Standard
Premium

explanation: A share change compares each plan with the total in the same year, so compute the totals for both years first. Totals: 2022 920, 2024 1220. Shares 2022 -> 2024: Basic 56.5% -> 47.5%, Standard 33.7% -> 36.9%, Premium 9.8% -> 15.6%. Standard gains 3.2 points versus Premium's 5.8, so blank 1 is Premium. Basic gained 60 thousand subscribers yet lost share, because the total grew faster than Basic did. Total growth = (1220 - 920) ÷ 920 ≈ 32.6%.

chart.title: Monthly sales of a regional bakery chain

intro: The chart shows monthly sales for the first nine months of the year.
text: [[1]] of the nine months had sales above the nine-month average, and sales grew at an average compound monthly rate of about [[2]]% from January to September.
explanation: Blank 1 needs the mean of all nine bars; blank 2 needs a compound rate over the eight steps between them. The sum is 2207, so the average is 245.2 thousand. Months above it: Jun 262, Jul 255, Aug 281, Sep 290, which is 4. April (245) is just below. From January to September there are 8 monthly steps: (290 ÷ 210)^(1/8) - 1 ≈ 4.12%. Dividing the total 38.1% gain by 8 without compounding gives about 4.8%, which is the trap.

chart.title: Price index for two housing markets (2015 = 100)

intro: Both indexes are set to 100 in 2015, so each value shows prices relative to that year.
text: Market B's prices first reached double their 2015 level in [[1]], and between 2020 and 2024 Market A's prices rose by about [[2]]%.
explanation: An index of 200 means double the base. Market B is 196 in 2022 and 212 in 2023, so it first reaches 200 in 2023; Market A reaches 201 only in 2024. For blank 2, compute the percent change between two index values rather than subtracting: (201 - 148) ÷ 148 ≈ 35.8%, about 36%. Reading the 53-point difference as 53% is the trap, valid only when the base is 100.

intro: A bank surveyed 900 store customers, 400 online customers and 200 phone customers. Each channel's bars sum to 100%.
text: Across all 1,500 respondents, about [[1]]% were very satisfied, and the share of phone respondents who were satisfied or very satisfied is [[2]] percentage points lower than the share for store respondents.
explanation: When groups differ in size, an overall percentage must be weighted by the number of respondents in each group. Weight by channel size: very satisfied = 900 × 0.42 + 400 × 0.28 + 200 × 0.18 = 378 + 112 + 36 = 526; 526 ÷ 1,500 = 35.1%, about 35%. The simple average of 42, 28 and 18 is about 29%, which ignores the different sample sizes. For blank 2, store satisfied-or-better = 42 + 33 = 75%, phone = 18 + 32 = 50%, a difference of 25 points.

chart.title: Fertilizer dose vs. crop yield, test plots

intro: An agronomist applied a different fertilizer dose to each of ten test plots.
text: Each additional unit of fertilizer is associated with roughly [[1]] kg more yield, and if the linear trend continued, a dose of 12 units would yield about [[2]] kg.
explanation: The points rise almost in a straight line from 3.1 at dose 1 to 11.2 at dose 10, a gain of 8.1 over 9 units, about 0.9 kg per unit (best-fit slope 0.88). Extending the line two more units from about 11.2: 11.2 + 2 × 0.9 ≈ 13.0 (the fitted line gives 12.76). Extrapolating beyond tested doses is risky in practice, but the question asks only about the trend.

chart.title: Annual recurring revenue of a software firm

intro: The chart shows a company's annual recurring revenue at year-end.
text: From 2019 to 2024 ARR grew at a compound annual rate of about [[1]]%, and if that rate continued, ARR at the end of 2026 would be about [[2]] million dollars.
explanation: Steadily rising increments on a line chart usually signal a constant percent growth rate rather than constant dollar growth. Growth factor over five years = 7.4 ÷ 2.0 = 3.7. The annual rate solves (1 + r)⁵ = 3.7, giving r ≈ 29.9%, about 30%. Check: 1.3⁵ ≈ 3.71. The trap 54% divides the 270% total gain by 5. Two more years at 1.3 each: 7.4 × 1.69 ≈ 12.5 million. Adding the 2023 to $2024 increase twice (7.4 + 2 × 1.7 = 10.8) underestimates compound growth.

intro: A furniture maker breaks down the cost of producing one chair.
text: From 2022 to 2024, unit cost rose by about [[1]]%, and materials accounted for about [[2]]% of that increase.
explanation: Add the four segments to get each year's unit cost. Separate the share of the increase from each component's own growth rate; they answer different questions. Totals: 2022 = 14.0 + 9.0 + 3.0 + 4.0 = 30.0; 2024 = 17.2 + 9.8 + 4.2 + 4.1 = 35.3. Percent rise = 5.3 ÷ 30 ≈ 17.7%. Materials rose by 3.2 of the $5.3 total increase, so 3.2 ÷ 5.3 ≈ 60%. The trap 23% is materials' own growth rate (3.2 ÷ 14). Energy spiked in 2023 but contributes only $1.2 over the full period.

chart.title: Outdoor temperature vs. daily heating gas use

intro: A building manager recorded gas use on nine days with different average outdoor temperatures.
text: The correlation between temperature and gas use is closest to [[1]], and extending the linear trend, a day averaging 70°F would use about [[2]] therms.
explanation: The points fall in a tight, nearly straight downward line, so the correlation is strongly negative, about -0.995, closest to -0.99. The best-fit slope is about -1.18 therms per degree: across 40 degrees use falls by 46, about 1.15 per degree. From 72 therms at 60°F, ten more degrees gives about 72 - 11.5 ≈ 60; the fitted line gives 59.4, closest to 58. Real heating use cannot fall below zero, so long extrapolations would eventually fail.

intro: A company compares each department's annual budget with actual spending.
text: [[1]] departments overspent their budget by more than 10%, and company-wide actual spending exceeded the total budget by about [[2]]%.
explanation: Compare actual with budget for each department as a percent of that department's budget. Variance = (actual - budget) ÷ budget: Ops 5.5%, IT 15.9%, HR -5.7%, Marketing 13.8%, R&D 7.3%, Facilities -2.4%. Only IT and Marketing exceed 10%, so blank 1 is 2. R&D has the largest dollar overrun (80) but only 7.3%. Totals: budget 3,600, actual 3,868; overrun 268 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 7.4%. Averaging the six percentages (about 5.7%) would be wrong, because departments differ in size.

intro: Both cities have grown at a nearly constant percent rate since 2016.
text: Over 2016-2024 Westfield grew at about [[1]]% per year, and if both cities keep their 2016-2024 compound growth rates, Westfield's population will first exceed Eastport's in about [[2]].
explanation: Westfield: 455 ÷ 300 ≈ 1.517 over 8 years, so r = 1.517^(1/8) - 1 ≈ 5.34%. Eastport: 562 ÷ 480 ≈ 1.171, r ≈ 1.99%. The gap ratio 562 ÷ 455 ≈ 1.235 closes by a factor of about 1.0535 ÷ 1.0199 ≈ 1.033 per year, and ln 1.235 ÷ ln 1.033 ≈ 6.5 years, so Westfield first exceeds Eastport about 6.5 years after 2024, in 2031 (year-by-year compounding confirms it). Extending the straight-line gains (about 10 and 19 thousand per year) would wrongly give about 2036, since it ignores compounding.

stem: A stationery shop sells pens for $3 each and notebooks for $5 each. A customer bought 11 items in total, some pens and some notebooks, and paid exactly $41. In the table, select the number of pens the customer bought and the number of notebooks the customer bought. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Let p be the number of pens and n the number of notebooks. Then p + n = 11 and 3p + 5n = 41. Substitute n = 11 - p: 3p + 55 - 5p = 41, so -2p = -14 and p = 7. Then n = 11 - 7 = 4. Check: 7 × 3 + 4 × 5 = 21 + 20 = 41. A quick alternative is to start with all 11 items as pens ($33); each swap of a pen for a notebook adds $2, and you need $8 more, so make 4 swaps: 4 notebooks and 7 pens.
trap: Choosing 4 pens and 7 notebooks reverses the roles; that combination costs 12 + 35 = $47, not $41.

stem: A café chain reports: "In the three months after we installed self-order kiosks in our downtown store, the store's average order value was 12 percent higher than in the three months before installation. The kiosks therefore raised average order value." In the table, select the statement that would most strengthen the chain's conclusion and the statement that would most weaken it. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: The chain plans to install kiosks in its suburban stores next year.
Average order value at the chain's other downtown stores, none of which has kiosks, did not change over the same six months.
Several customers said that they found the kiosks easy to use.
The kiosks were installed in the same week that the chain raised its menu prices by about 12 percent.
The number of customers served each day at the downtown store rose slightly after the kiosks were installed.
explanation: The argument infers cause from a before-and-after change at one store. A strengthener rules out other explanations for the rise: if comparable downtown stores without kiosks saw no change over the same period, general trends such as seasonality or a downtown boom are less likely to explain the 12 percent rise. A weakener offers another cause: a menu price increase of about 12 percent, made at the same time, could by itself produce a 12 percent higher order value with no help from the kiosks. The customer count concerns how many people ordered, not how much each order was worth. Ease of use and expansion plans do not bear on whether the kiosks caused the rise.
trap: The rise in daily customers looks relevant, but the conclusion is about value per order, not number of orders.

stem: A community theater sold 20 tickets for a matinee. Adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $7, and ticket revenue for the matinee was $190. In the table, select the number of adult tickets sold and the number of child tickets sold. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Let a be adult tickets and c child tickets. Then a + c = 20 and 12a + 7c = 190. If all 20 tickets were child tickets, revenue would be 20 × 7 = $140. Each adult ticket adds $5 more than a child ticket, and the actual revenue is $50 higher, so a = 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Then c = 20 - 10 = 10. Check: 120 + 70 = 190. Both columns take the same value, which is allowed in Two-Part Analysis.
trap: Test-takers often assume the two answers must differ and pick 12 and 8, which gives 144 + 56 = $200.

stem: A library board member wrote: "Riverside Library should extend its weekend opening hours. Over the past two years, weekend visits have grown by 30 percent while weekday visits have declined. A staff survey also found that most employees would accept weekend shifts in exchange for a free weekday." In the table, select the statement that is the main conclusion of the argument and the statement that is offered as evidence for that conclusion. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Weekday visits to the library will continue to decline.
Most library employees prefer weekday shifts to weekend shifts.
Weekend visits to the library have grown by 30 percent over the past two years.
Extending weekend hours will cost less than the board expects.
Riverside Library should extend its weekend opening hours.
explanation: The main conclusion is the claim the rest of the passage is meant to support: the library should extend its weekend hours. The growth in weekend visits is stated as a fact and is given as a reason for the change, so it is evidence. The claim that weekday visits will continue to decline is a prediction the author never makes; the passage reports only a past decline. The statement about staff preferring weekday shifts goes beyond the survey, which says only that staff would accept weekend shifts for a trade. Nothing in the passage mentions costs.
trap: The prediction about weekday visits sounds like part of the reasoning, but the author describes only what has already happened.

stem: A company's combined quarterly budget for its Marketing and Operations departments is $30,000. The Marketing budget is $8,000 more than the Operations budget. In the table, select the Marketing budget and the Operations budget, in thousands of dollars. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Let M and O be the budgets in thousands. M + O = 30 and M - O = 8. Adding the two equations gives 2M = 38, so M = 19. Then O = 30 - 19 = 11. Check: 19 - 11 = 8. A fast mental route: split the total evenly (15 each), then move half of the difference (4) from one side to the other: 15 + 4 = 19 and 15 - 4 = 11.
trap: Selecting 22 and 8 uses the difference as one of the budgets; 8 is not even an option, and 22 + 8 is 30 but 22 - 8 is 14, not 8.

stem: A plant has two machines. Machine A produces 45 units per hour and Machine B produces 30 units per hour. For one order, the two machines together ran for a total of 13 machine-hours (hours of A plus hours of B) and produced exactly 465 units. In the table, select the number of hours Machine A ran and the number of hours Machine B ran. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Let a and b be the hours for A and B. Then a + b = 13 and 45a + 30b = 465. If B ran all 13 hours, output would be 13 × 30 = 390 units. Each hour shifted from B to A adds 15 units, and 465 - 390 = 75 extra units are needed, so a = 75 ÷ 15 = 5. Then b = 13 - 5 = 8. Check: 45 × 5 + 30 × 8 = 225 + 240 = 465.
trap: Picking 8 hours for A and 5 for B swaps the machines and gives 360 + 150 = 510 units.

stem: A software company's chief operating officer argues: "Last quarter, a pilot group of 40 engineers moved to a four-day, 32-hour week and shipped as many product features as they had in the previous quarter. Therefore, moving the entire 600-person company to a four-day week will not reduce our output." In the table, select the assumption on which the argument depends and the finding that would most weaken the argument. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: The pilot group shipped more features than any other engineering team last quarter.
The engineers in the pilot were chosen at random from across the engineering department.
Most employees outside the pilot group would prefer a four-day week.
The way the pilot engineers' output responded to fewer hours is representative of how output across the rest of the company would respond.
During the pilot, other teams quietly took over the pilot group's support and maintenance work.
None of the company's main competitors has adopted a four-day week.
explanation: The argument generalises from 40 engineers to all 600 staff, many of whom do different kinds of work. It must therefore assume that the pilot group's response to fewer hours is typical of the company; if it is not, the pilot result tells us little. The weakener reveals that the pilot result itself is misleading: if other teams absorbed the pilot group's support work, the engineers had more time for features, and company-wide output did not really hold steady. Random selection within engineering would slightly support the argument, not undermine it. Employee preferences, the group's relative productivity and competitors' policies do not affect whether output would fall.
trap: Random selection of pilot engineers sounds like the needed assumption, but it is not required, and it covers only engineers rather than the whole company.

stem: A roaster blends a house coffee costing $8 per pound with a premium coffee costing $14 per pound to make 30 pounds of a blend whose ingredient cost averages exactly $10 per pound. In the table, select the number of pounds of house coffee and the number of pounds of premium coffee used. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Use the weighted-average idea. The target $10 is $2 above the house price and $4 below the premium price, so the amounts are in the inverse ratio 4 : 2, that is, house : premium = 2 : 1. Of 30 pounds, house coffee is 20 and premium is 10. Algebra check: 8h + 14p = 30 × 10 = 300 and h + p = 30, so 8h + 420 - 14h = 300, giving h = 20 and p = 10.
trap: Choosing 10 pounds of house and 20 of premium applies the distances directly instead of inversely, which gives an average of $12 per pound.

stem: Last year a regional grocery chain's revenue rose 15 percent, but its net profit fell 10 percent. In the table, select the statement that would best help explain the rise in revenue and the statement that would best help explain the fall in profit. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: The number of members in the chain's loyalty programme did not change during the year.
Several customers praised the chain's new in-store bakery.
The chain operated the same number of stores at the end of the year as at the start.
The chain's electricity and refrigeration costs more than doubled after a fixed-price energy contract expired.
The chain raised shelf prices by about 14 percent during the year, in line with regional food inflation.
The chain moved its head office to a smaller building with lower rent.
explanation: Revenue is price times volume, so a roughly 14 percent rise in shelf prices accounts for most of a 15 percent revenue increase even if the number of items sold was flat. Profit is revenue minus costs, so profit can fall while revenue rises only if costs rose faster; a more than doubling of energy and refrigeration costs, a major expense for a grocer, explains that. Lower office rent would raise profit, the opposite of what needs explaining. Unchanged loyalty membership and an unchanged store count explain neither change. Praise for the bakery is too vague to account for a 15 percent revenue jump.
trap: The lower head-office rent concerns costs, but it would push profit up, not down.

stem: A cloud storage plan charges a fixed monthly fee plus a constant charge per gigabyte (GB) stored. A client stored 120 GB in March and was billed $410; the client stored 200 GB in April and was billed $570. In the table, select the fixed monthly fee, in dollars, and the charge per GB, in dollars. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: The fixed fee is the same both months, so the change in the bill comes only from the extra storage. April used 200 - 120 = 80 more GB and cost 570 - 410 = $160 more, so the rate is 160 ÷ 80 = $2 per GB. Then the fixed fee is 410 - 120 × 2 = 410 - 240 = $170. Check with April: 170 + 200 × 2 = 570.
trap: Dividing a single bill by its storage (410 ÷ 120, about 3.4) ignores the fixed fee and suggests the $3 rate.

stem: At Halvorsen Logistics, every driver who completed the advanced safety course last year received a bonus. No driver who had an accident last year received a bonus. Some drivers who received a bonus work night shifts. In the table, select the statement that must be true if the information above is true and the statement that cannot be true if the information above is true. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: One driver both completed the advanced safety course and had an accident last year.
Every driver who received a bonus completed the advanced safety course.
Some night-shift drivers had accidents last year.
All night-shift drivers received a bonus.
Some night-shift drivers did not complete the advanced safety course.
No driver who completed the advanced safety course had an accident last year.
explanation: Chain the two rules. Course completed -> bonus, and accident -> no bonus, which is equivalent to bonus -> no accident. So course completed -> bonus -> no accident: no course completer had an accident. That must be true, and its direct contradiction, a driver who completed the course and had an accident, cannot be true. The claim that every bonus recipient completed the course reverses the first rule, so it might be false but could also be true. The statements about night-shift drivers are all possible: the information says only that some bonus recipients work nights, which leaves room for other night-shift drivers to have had accidents, to have skipped the course, or even for all of them to have received bonuses.
trap: Every bonus recipient completing the course feels required, but the rule runs only from course to bonus, not from bonus to course.

stem: Two board members of a regional airline disagree about replacing its 50-seat turboprop aircraft with 120-seat jets. Ms. Ortiz argues that the switch will raise profit because larger jets have a lower operating cost per seat. Mr. Bell argues that the switch will lower profit on most of the airline's routes. In the table, select the finding that would most support Ms. Ortiz's position and the finding that would most support Mr. Bell's position. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: On most of the airline's routes, the turboprops fly about half full even at peak times.
Fuel prices have been stable for the past two years.
On most of the airline's routes, the turboprops already fly with over 90 percent of seats filled, and passengers are regularly turned away.
The airline's pilots would need several weeks of training to fly the jets.
The airline's main airport plans to raise landing fees by the same percentage for all aircraft.
explanation: A lower cost per seat helps only if the extra seats are sold. If the turboprops are almost always full and passengers are turned away, there is unmet demand that larger jets could capture, so Ortiz's cost advantage would turn into higher profit. If the turboprops fly half full, a 120-seat jet would fly mostly empty, so the cost per passenger, not per seat, would rise and profit would fall, which supports Bell. Stable fuel prices affect both aircraft types similarly. A few weeks of training is a one-time cost that does not decide the long-run question. Equal percentage fee rises affect both options in the same proportion.
trap: Pilot retraining is a cost of switching, but it is small and temporary next to the route-by-route load factors.

stem: A retailer marks up the cost of a jacket by m percent to set its list price and later sells it at a discount of d percent off the list price. The final selling price is exactly 20 percent above the retailer's cost, and the discount percent d is exactly 30 less than the markup percent m. In the table, select the markup percent and the discount percent. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: The price multipliers must satisfy (1 + m/100)(1 - d/100) = 1.2 with d = m - 30. Test the options in pairs that differ by 30: (40, 10) gives 1.4 × 0.9 = 1.26; (50, 20) gives 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.20, which works. Algebraically, with m as a decimal, (1 + m)(1.3 - m) = 1.2 simplifies to m² - 0.3m - 0.1 = 0, whose only positive root is m = 0.5. So the markup is 50 percent and the discount 20 percent.
trap: The pair 60 and 25 also gives a 20 percent gain (1.6 × 0.75 = 1.2), but the two percents differ by 35, not 30.

stem: A workplace study found that office workers who used standing desks reported 20 percent fewer back complaints over a year than workers who used conventional desks. The researchers concluded that using a standing desk reduces back problems. In the table, select the statement that would most strengthen the researchers' conclusion and the statement that would most weaken it. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: The study included workers from several different companies.
Standing desks cost about twice as much as conventional desks.
Many workers who used standing desks reported more leg fatigue than other workers.
Workers in the study chose their own desks, and those who already had back pain mostly avoided standing desks because standing was uncomfortable for them.
Back complaints were measured by the same questionnaire for all participants.
In a follow-up, workers assigned at random to switch to standing desks reported fewer back complaints over the next year than colleagues who kept conventional desks.
explanation: The study compares self-selected groups, so the key alternative explanation is that people with healthier backs chose standing desks. A randomised follow-up removes that self-selection: if randomly assigned standing-desk users still report fewer complaints, the desk itself is the most plausible cause. The weakener supplies exactly the self-selection story: if people with back pain avoided standing desks, the conventional-desk group started with more back problems, which could produce the 20 percent gap without any effect from the desks. Cost and leg fatigue are irrelevant to whether back problems fall. Using the same questionnaire and including several companies offer only minor support, much weaker than random assignment.
trap: Including several companies sounds like support, but it addresses how widely the result applies, not whether the desks caused it.

stem: An event planner will seat exactly 100 guests using round tables that seat 8 and square tables that seat 6, with every seat at every table filled. The planner wants to use the smallest possible total number of tables. In the table, select the number of 8-seat tables and the number of 6-seat tables in the planner's arrangement. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Solve 8x + 6y = 100, or 4x + 3y = 50, in non-negative integers. Then 50 - 4x must be divisible by 3, so x = 2, 5, 8 or 11, giving y = 14, 10, 6 or 2. The totals are 16, 15, 14 and 13 tables. Because larger tables reduce the count, the minimum uses as many 8-seat tables as possible: 11 tables of 8 and 2 tables of 6, for 13 tables. Check: 88 + 12 = 100.
trap: The pair 8 and 6 also seats exactly 100 guests, but it uses 14 tables rather than the minimum 13.

stem: The city accepts bids for its transit maintenance contract only from vendors that hold a national safety certification. Only firms with at least five years of operating history hold this certification. The city has accepted a bid from Ferrovia Services. In the table, select the statement that must be true if the information above is true and the statement that, if true, would show that at least one statement above is false. Make only two selections, one in each column.
cols: Would show a statement above is false
options: Ferrovia Services submitted the lowest bid the city received.
The city has rejected at least one bid for the contract.
Every firm with at least five years of operating history holds the certification.
Ferrovia Services has at least five years of operating history.
Some certified firms did not bid for the contract.
Ferrovia Services has been operating for only three years.
explanation: Follow the chain: the bid was accepted -> Ferrovia holds the certification (only certified vendors' bids are accepted) -> Ferrovia has at least five years of operating history (only such firms hold it). So the five-year statement must be true. A statement that Ferrovia has been operating for only three years is incompatible with that result, so if it were true, one of the three original statements would have to be false. The claim that every five-year firm is certified reverses the second rule and is not guaranteed. The lowest-bid claim, uncertified non-bidders and rejected bids are all consistent with the information but not required by it.
trap: The claim that every five-year firm holds the certification reverses the second rule, which says only that certification requires five years.

stem: Working together at their constant rates, Pump A and Pump B can drain a reservoir in 6 hours. Working alone, Pump A takes 5 fewer hours than Pump B to drain the reservoir. In the table, select the number of hours Pump A takes alone and the number of hours Pump B takes alone. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Only one pair of options differs by exactly 5 hours: 10 and 15. Check the combined rate: 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, so together they take 6 hours, as required. Algebraically, 1/a + 1/(a + 5) = 1/6 leads to a² - 7a - 30 = 0, or (a - 10)(a + 3) = 0, so a = 10 and b = 15.
trap: Picking 12 and 12 treats the pumps as equal (each half of the work doubles 6 hours), ignoring that A is 5 hours faster.

stem: An analyst wrote: "Some investors expect Taluna's share price to fall because its largest customer is switching suppliers. They point out that 'losing that customer will cut Taluna's revenue by about a fifth.' This view overlooks Taluna's new contract with a national retailer, which alone should replace the lost revenue within a year. So 'Taluna's revenue outlook does not justify a lower share price.'" In the table, select the role played in the analyst's argument by the first quoted claim and the role played by the second quoted claim. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: It is an intermediate conclusion that the analyst supports with further evidence and then uses to support the main conclusion.
It is evidence the analyst uses to support the main conclusion.
It is a consideration offered in support of a position that the analyst rejects.
It is the main conclusion of the analyst's argument.
It is a finding that the analyst argues is inaccurate.
explanation: The investors' position is that the share price will fall, and the first quoted claim, the expected one-fifth revenue cut, is their reason. The analyst does not dispute the revenue cut; the analyst argues that it will be offset by the new retail contract. So the first claim supports a position the analyst rejects, but it is not itself argued to be inaccurate. The second quoted claim follows from the offset argument and is introduced by 'So', with nothing further built on it; it is the main conclusion. It is not merely evidence, and it is not an intermediate step toward some further claim.
trap: Calling the first claim a finding the analyst argues is inaccurate is tempting, but the analyst accepts the revenue cut and disputes only what it implies for the share price.

stem: An investor divided $10,000 between a savings account paying 4 percent simple annual interest and a bond fund paying 7 percent simple annual interest. After one year the two investments together earned $580 in interest. In the table, select the amount invested in the savings account and the amount invested in the bond fund. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: The blended return is 580 ÷ 10,000 = 5.8 percent. That is 1.8 points above 4 percent and 1.2 points below 7 percent, so the amounts are in the inverse ratio savings : bond = 1.2 : 1.8 = 2 : 3. Split $10,000 in the ratio 2 : 3 to get $4,000 in savings and $6,000 in the bond fund. Check: 160 + 420 = 580.
trap: Choosing $6,000 in savings and $4,000 in bonds reverses the inverse ratio and earns only 240 + 280 = $520.

stem: A marine biologist hypothesises that the recent decline in parrotfish on Kerrin Reef has been caused mainly by increased sediment runoff from a new coastal resort rather than by fishing. In the table, select the finding that would most support the biologist's hypothesis and the finding that would most undermine it. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Parrotfish numbers fell by a similar amount over the same period at a distant reef where sediment levels have not changed and no development has occurred.
Several other fish species on Kerrin Reef have had stable populations.
The resort employs a marine biologist to monitor the reef.
The parrotfish decline has been sharpest on the sections of the reef nearest the resort's drainage outlets and mildest on the sections farthest from them.
The resort opened two years ago.
explanation: A causal hypothesis is supported when the effect tracks the proposed cause. If the decline is steepest near the drainage outlets and weakest far from them, the pattern matches the spread of sediment, which supports the runoff explanation. It is undermined when the effect appears without the cause: a similar decline on a distant reef with no new sediment suggests that some wider factor, such as fishing or water temperature, is at work. The opening date, the stability of other species and the resort's monitoring staff do not distinguish runoff from other causes.
trap: Stable populations of other species can look like evidence against sediment, but sediment may affect parrotfish and their food without harming every species.

stem: A training center books its seminar room only in blocks of 45 minutes or 75 minutes. Last week the room was booked for exactly 600 minutes in total, using at least one block of each length. Among all combinations that satisfy these conditions, the number of 75-minute blocks was as large as possible. In the table, select the number of 45-minute blocks and the number of 75-minute blocks booked. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Divide 45a + 75b = 600 by 15 to get 3a + 5b = 40. Then 40 - 5b must be a positive multiple of 3. b = 2 gives a = 10; b = 5 gives a = 5; b = 8 gives a = 0, which is not allowed because at least one 45-minute block was used. So the largest possible b is 5, with a = 5. Both columns take the value 5.
trap: Choosing 0 and 8 maximises the 75-minute blocks but breaks the at-least-one-of-each condition, and 0 is not offered; 10 and 2 satisfy the total but do not maximise the 75-minute blocks.

stem: Each day a bakery makes only cakes and pies. A cake earns $12 profit and uses 3 oven-hours and 1 labor-hour. A pie earns $8 profit and uses 1 oven-hour and 2 labor-hours. The bakery has at most 30 oven-hours and 28 labor-hours per day and makes only whole items. In the table, select the number of cakes and the number of pies that give the greatest possible daily profit. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Profit peaks where both limits are nearly used. Solving 3c + p = 30 and c + 2p = 28 gives c = 6.4 and p = 10.8, so check whole numbers nearby. (6, 11): oven 18 + 11 = 29, labor 6 + 22 = 28, profit 72 + 88 = $160. (7, 9): oven 30, labor 25, profit 84 + 72 = $156. (6, 10): profit $152. (7, 10) needs 31 oven-hours, too many. (5, 11) earns only $148 and (5, 12) needs 29 labor-hours. The maximum is 6 cakes and 11 pies.
trap: Rounding the corner point to 7 cakes and 9 pies feels natural, but it earns $156, less than the $160 from 6 cakes and 11 pies.

stem: Manager: "Customer cancellations rose sharply in the quarter after we cut our support team by a third. Restoring the support team to its former size will bring cancellations back down." Analyst: "Cancellations rose because a cheaper competitor launched that same quarter. Restoring the support team will not reduce cancellations." In the table, select the assumption on which the manager's argument depends and the assumption on which the analyst's argument depends. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: The competitor will soon raise its prices.
The competitor's product is cheaper than the company's product.
The support team was cut by more than half.
Customers who cancelled would have left even if support had remained as good as it was before the cuts.
At least some of the customers who cancelled did so partly because support became slower or worse after the cuts.
Cancellations will keep rising next year unless the company acts.
explanation: The manager infers from timing that the support cuts caused the rise and that reversing them will reverse it. That requires that worse support drove at least some cancellations; if no one left because of support, restoring the team cannot help. The analyst claims restoring the team will not reduce cancellations at all, which requires that the departing customers would have left anyway even with the old level of support. Negating that assumption, so that better support would have kept some customers, destroys the analyst's claim. The competitor being cheaper is stated by the analyst, not assumed. The size of the cut (a third, not more than half), future trends and competitor pricing are not needed by either argument.
trap: The competitor being cheaper looks central to the analyst's case, but the analyst states it outright, so it is a premise rather than an unstated assumption.

stem: A firm's analytics staff is split into Group A, whose average annual salary is $55,000, and Group B, whose average annual salary is $70,000. The average salary of all analytics staff is $62,000, and the total annual payroll for analytics staff is $1.86 million. In the table, select the number of staff in Group A and the number in Group B. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: First find the headcount: 1,860,000 ÷ 62,000 = 30 staff. Next use the weighted average. The overall $62,000 is 7 thousand above Group A and 8 thousand below Group B, so A : B = 8 : 7 (inverse ratio). With 30 staff, A = 30 × 8/15 = 16 and B = 14. Check: 16 × 55 + 14 × 70 = 880 + 980 = 1,860 thousand.
trap: Using the distances directly gives A : B = 7 : 8, or 14 and 16, which would put the average above $62,500.

stem: In the twelve months after Harbor City introduced a charge for driving into its central zone, the number of cars entering the zone fell 18 percent compared with the previous twelve months. The mayor concluded that the charge reduced traffic into the zone. In the table, select the statement that would most strengthen the mayor's conclusion and the statement that would most weaken it. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Over the same two years, car entries into the central zones of three comparable cities without such charges were essentially unchanged.
The city's population grew slightly over the two years.
The charge took effect in the same month that the zone's largest office complex, employing about a fifth of the zone's workers, closed for two years of renovation.
The charge is higher on weekdays than at weekends.
Surveys show that many drivers dislike the charge.
Revenue from the charge is being used to build new bus lanes outside the zone.
explanation: The mayor attributes an 18 percent fall to the charge, so the key question is whether something else could explain it. Comparable cities without the charge showing no change make broad causes, such as fuel prices or a regional slowdown, unlikely, which strengthens the conclusion. Closing an office complex that employed about a fifth of the zone's workers at the same moment would by itself cut commuter trips into the zone by a large amount, offering a strong rival explanation. Slight population growth would, if anything, make the fall more impressive, but its effect is small and indirect. Bus lanes outside the zone, driver attitudes and weekday pricing do not test whether the charge caused the fall.
trap: Population growth seems to strengthen the conclusion, but a slight rise is a much weaker control than the comparison with cities that had no charge.

stem: A courier drove 120 kilometres from a depot to a client at a constant speed and returned along the same route at a different constant speed that was 20 kilometres per hour faster. The average speed for the whole round trip was 48 kilometres per hour. In the table, select the speed on the outbound trip and the speed on the return trip, in kilometres per hour. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: The round trip is 240 km at an average of 48 km/h, so it took 5 hours. Only one option pair differs by exactly 20, namely (40, 60), so test it: 120/40 + 120/60 = 3 + 2 = 5 hours. That works. Algebraically, 120/u + 120/(u + 20) = 5 gives u² - 28u - 480 = 0, or (u - 40)(u + 12) = 0, so u = 40 and the return speed is 60.
trap: Averaging the speeds simply, (u + u + 20)/2 = 48, gives 38 and 58; the arithmetic mean is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed.

stem: Argument 1: "Seventy percent of the five-star reviews of our app mention the new dark mode, so dark mode is the feature most of our users value most." Argument 2: "Sales regions where we ran podcast advertising last year grew faster than regions where we did not, so podcast advertising caused the faster growth." In the table, select the flaw that most accurately describes Argument 1 and the flaw that most accurately describes Argument 2. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: It relies on a key term that is used in two different senses.
It treats the absence of evidence against a claim as proof that the claim is true.
It draws a conclusion about a whole population from a sample that may not be representative of it.
It assumes that what is true of a group as a whole must be true of each member of the group.
It presents a conclusion that merely restates one of its premises.
It assumes that because two things occurred together, one must have caused the other.
explanation: Argument 1 moves from five-star reviewers to most users. People who post five-star reviews are a self-selected, enthusiastic subset, so their comments may not reflect what typical users value: an unrepresentative-sample flaw. Argument 2 observes that podcast regions grew faster and concludes that the podcasts caused it, without ruling out other differences, such as the company having chosen regions that were already growing for the campaign: a correlation-to-causation flaw. Neither argument shifts the meaning of a term, relies on missing counter-evidence, reasons from a group to its members, or simply restates a premise.
trap: Argument 1 can look like a group-to-member error, but it actually reasons from a part (reviewers) to the whole user base, which is a sampling problem.

stem: A company's revenue rose by p percent in 2024 and then fell by q percent in 2025, so that revenue at the end of 2025 was exactly equal to revenue at the start of 2024. The percent increase p was 5 points larger than the percent decrease q. In the table, select the value of p and the value of q. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Returning to the start requires (1 + p/100)(1 - q/100) = 1. Pairs that differ by 5: (20, 15) gives 1.2 × 0.85 = 1.02, too high; (25, 20) gives 1.25 × 0.8 = 1.00, exact; (30, 25) is not available. So p = 25 and q = 20. Note the general rule: undoing an increase of p percent needs a decrease of p/(100 + p) × 100 percent, here 25/125 = 20 percent.
trap: The pair 33⅓ and 25 also restores the original revenue (4/3 × 3/4 = 1), but the two values differ by 8⅓, not 5.

stem: Select for blank (1) and blank (2) the options that best complete the passage. "In a trial, a bank sent a text reminder three days before the due date to a randomly chosen half of its credit-card customers and sent no reminder to the other half. Customers in the reminded group paid late 40 percent less often than those in the other group. The trial therefore supports the conclusion that ___(1)___. However, extending the reminders to all customers would be justified on financial grounds only if ___(2)___." Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: text reminders reduce the likelihood of late payment among customers like those in the trial
the savings to the bank from fewer late payments exceed the cost of sending the reminders, including any late fees the bank would no longer collect
late fees are the bank's largest single source of profit
customers prefer text messages to e-mail reminders
customers who pay late do so because they forget the due date
the reminded group contained more high-income customers than the other group
explanation: Because customers were assigned at random, the two groups should be alike except for the reminder, so the trial supports a causal conclusion limited to similar customers: reminders reduce late payment. 'Customers who pay late do so because they forget' overstates the finding; reminders could work for other reasons and need not explain every late payment. Random assignment makes it unlikely that one group had more high-income customers. For the second blank, a financial justification needs benefits that exceed costs; the correct option also recognises that the bank loses some late-fee income, which is a real cost of the plan. Saying that late fees are the bank's largest profit source is a point against the rollout, not a condition for it.
trap: The forgetting option sounds like a natural explanation, but the trial shows only that reminders reduce late payment, not why every customer pays late.

stem: A theater currently charges $20 per ticket and sells 400 tickets per show. Market research shows that for every $1 increase in price, 10 fewer tickets are sold, and for every $1 decrease, 10 more are sold. Each ticket sold also carries a $4 cost for staffing and programs. Prices are whole dollars. In the table, select the ticket price that maximises profit per show and the number of tickets sold at that price. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: Let k be the price increase in dollars. Profit = (20 + k - 4)(400 - 10k) = (16 + k)(400 - 10k). This is a downward parabola with roots k = -16 and k = 40, so its maximum is midway, at k = (-16 + 40)/2 = 12. The price is 20 + 12 = $32 and tickets sold are 400 - 120 = 280. Profit is 28 × 280 = $7,840; compare k = 10: 26 × 300 = $7,800, and k = 14: 30 × 260 = $7,800.
trap: Maximising revenue instead of profit gives k = 10, a price of $30 and 300 tickets; the $4 per-ticket cost pushes the best price higher.

stem: Lena: "Our startup should hire a head of sales now. The product is ready, and as long as the founders do all the selling, growth will be capped at the few deals we can close ourselves." Omar: "Hiring a head of sales now is premature. Until we know which customer segment buys fastest, a sales leader would build a team around the wrong customers." In the table, select the statement that Lena and Omar would most likely both agree with and the statement that is the point on which they disagree. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Choices about which customers to target shape how a sales team is built.
The startup should hire a head of sales at its current stage.
Selling done only by the founders will limit the company's growth indefinitely.
The startup will at some point need a head of sales.
The startup already knows which customer segment buys fastest.
The product is not yet ready to sell.
explanation: Omar calls the hire 'premature', which implies that it will be appropriate later, and Lena wants it now; so both accept that a head of sales will eventually be needed. Their disagreement is about timing: Lena says hire now and Omar says not yet. Omar never disputes that the product is ready, so that is not their point of disagreement. The indefinite limit from founder-led selling and the claim about how targeting shapes a team are each asserted by only one speaker, with the other silent. Omar implies the startup does not yet know its fastest segment, but Lena says nothing about it, so it is not a clear point of agreement or disagreement.
trap: The claim about targeting shaping a sales team is plausible to both, but only Omar commits to it; agreement questions need evidence from both speakers.

stem: A bag contains only red and blue chips. When two chips are drawn at random without replacement, the probability that both are red is 1/3 and the probability that both are blue is 2/15. In the table, select the number of red chips and the number of blue chips in the bag. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: With n chips, P(both red) = r(r - 1)/[n(n - 1)] = 1/3 and P(both blue) = b(b - 1)/[n(n - 1)] = 2/15. The denominator n(n - 1) must be a multiple of 15 and of 3; try n = 10, so n(n - 1) = 90. Then r(r - 1) = 30, giving r = 6, and b(b - 1) = 12, giving b = 4. Indeed 6 + 4 = 10. Check: 30/90 = 1/3 and 12/90 = 2/15. Testing option pairs directly also works: only (6, 4) satisfies both probabilities.
trap: Choosing 15 blue chips comes from a 36-chip bag with 21 red, which meets the red condition but makes both-blue 1/6, not 2/15.

stem: A retailer's marketing director notes that members of its loyalty programme spend, on average, 35 percent more per year at its stores than non-members do. She concludes that the programme causes customers to spend more. In the table, select the statement that would most strengthen her conclusion and the statement that would most weaken it. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Customers who joined the programme increased their annual spending by about 30 percent in the year after joining, while the spending of otherwise similar non-members was flat over the same period.
Members are more likely than non-members to shop on the retailer's website.
The programme has more members this year than it had last year.
The average member has belonged to the programme for four years.
Members receive a 5 percent discount on all purchases.
Before joining, customers who later became members already spent about 35 percent more per year than customers who never joined.
explanation: The comparison between members and non-members could reflect who joins rather than what the programme does. The best strengthener tracks the same customers before and after joining against a similar group that did not join: a 30 percent jump among joiners with flat spending among comparable non-members points to the programme as the cause. The best weakener shows that the whole 35 percent gap existed before anyone joined, which means heavy spenders select into the programme and the programme itself adds little. A 5 percent discount, growth in membership, online shopping habits and average tenure describe the programme or its members but do not separate cause from selection.
trap: The 5 percent discount seems to explain extra spending, but a discount lowers the price of each purchase and says nothing about whether members buy more because of it.

stem: A lab needs at least 50 litres of an acid solution that is at least 30 percent acid. It can buy only whole litres of Solution X, which is 20 percent acid and costs $2 per litre, and Solution Y, which is 50 percent acid and costs $5 per litre, and it will mix them. In the table, select the number of litres of X and the number of litres of Y in the cheapest purchase that meets both requirements. Make only two selections, one in each column.
explanation: The concentration condition is 0.2x + 0.5y ≥ 0.3(x + y), which simplifies to 0.2y ≥ 0.1x, or x ≤ 2y. X is cheaper, so use as much X as allowed and no more total than needed. With x + y = 50 and x ≤ 2y, y ≥ 16⅔, so y = 17 and x = 33 (33 ≤ 34). Cost: 66 + 85 = $151. Alternatives: (34, 17) costs $153 and (34, 16) violates x ≤ 2y. So 33 litres of X and 17 of Y.
trap: Solving x = 2y and x + y = 50 exactly gives fractions; rounding to 34 and 17 meets the requirements but costs $2 more than 33 and 17.

stem: In a recent hiring round at a consultancy, 60 percent of applicants who had an employee referral reached the interview stage, compared with 20 percent of applicants who had no referral. Applicants with a referral made up 10 percent of all applicants. In the table, select the statement that must be true based on this information and the statement that cannot be true based on this information. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: Some applicants who reached the interview stage were later rejected.
Referred applicants were, on average, better qualified than non-referred applicants.
Most applicants who reached the interview stage had a referral.
The consultancy will hire more referred applicants than non-referred applicants.
The consultancy received more applications this round than in the previous round.
Applicants with a referral made up exactly one quarter of the applicants who reached the interview stage.
explanation: Pick 100 applicants. Ten had a referral, and 60 percent of them, 6 people, were interviewed. Ninety had no referral, and 20 percent of them, 18 people, were interviewed. So 24 people reached interviews, of whom 6 ÷ 24 = 25 percent were referred: exactly one quarter, which must be true for any total. Because referred applicants are only a quarter of interviewees, the claim that most interviewees were referred cannot be true. The information says nothing about hiring decisions, qualifications, later rejections or previous rounds, so those statements could be true or false.
trap: A 60 percent versus 20 percent pass rate makes 'most interviewees were referred' feel right, but referred applicants were only 10 percent of the pool.

stem: A commentator wrote: "Ministry economists predicted that 'cutting the fuel tax would raise fuel consumption sharply.' Yet in the year after the cut, consumption barely changed. Some have taken this as proof that drivers do not respond to fuel prices. That inference is mistaken: 'the cut coincided with a sharp rise in world oil prices, so pump prices hardly fell,' and drivers had little to respond to." In the table, select the role played in the argument by the first quoted claim and the role played by the second quoted claim. Make only two selections, one in each column.
options: It is evidence offered to undermine an inference drawn from a particular outcome.
It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is a prediction whose apparent failure the commentator explains without giving up the view that drivers respond to price.
It is a generalisation that the commentator uses to support the main conclusion.
It is the claim that some people offer as proof that drivers ignore fuel prices.
It is an assumption on which the economists' prediction depended.
explanation: The commentator's main conclusion is 'That inference is mistaken', meaning the flat consumption does not prove drivers ignore prices. The first quoted claim is the economists' prediction; it apparently failed, and the commentator explains that failure in a way that keeps the idea that drivers respond to price. The second quoted claim, that pump prices hardly fell, is the evidence against the inference: drivers did not face lower prices, so their flat consumption says nothing about price sensitivity. Neither quote is the main conclusion. The proof offered by others is the flat consumption figure, not either quote. The second claim is a specific fact about one year, not a generalisation or the economists' assumption.
trap: Calling the second claim the main conclusion is tempting because it ends the argument, but it supports the earlier sentence 'That inference is mistaken'.

tabs.title: Procurement e-mail
tabs.text:
From: Dana Whitfield, Procurement Lead
To: Operations team

We need a supplier of replacement filter cartridges for our water-treatment units. Our annual requirement is 2,400 cartridges. Under company policy, a vendor qualifies only if its defect rate is below 1.5 percent and it can deliver within 10 business days of an order. Among qualifying vendors, we choose the one with the lowest first-year cost, defined as the unit price times 2,400 plus any one-time setup fee.

tabs.title: Finance memo
tabs.text: Vendors that offer 60-day payment terms receive a credit of 2 percent of their first-year cost when vendors are compared. Of the four vendors quoted, only ClearPath and Purus offer 60-day terms. Finance also asks that the chosen vendor's first-year cost, before any credit, not exceed $30,000.

questions.stem: If the procurement policy is applied and the finance memo is ignored, which vendor will be chosen?
questions.explanation: Purus fails the delivery rule (12 days) and Vantex fails the defect rule (1.6 percent), so only Aqualine and ClearPath qualify. First-year cost: Aqualine 2,400 × 11.50 + 1,800 = $29,400; ClearPath 2,400 × 10.90 + 3,500 = 26,160 + 3,500 = $29,660. Aqualine is cheaper by $260, so Aqualine is chosen. Purus has the lowest cost overall ($26,960), which is the trap; it does not qualify.

questions.stem: If the 2 percent credit in the finance memo is applied when comparing qualifying vendors, the chosen vendor's credited first-year cost will be lower than Aqualine's first-year cost by approximately how much?
questions.explanation: With the credit, ClearPath's comparison cost is 0.98 × 29,660 = $29,066.80. Aqualine has no credit and stays at $29,400, so ClearPath becomes the cheapest qualifying vendor. The difference is 29,400 - 29,066.80 = $333.20, about $333. The $260 option is the gap before the credit, in Aqualine's favour.

questions.prompt: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true based on the information provided. Otherwise select No.

statements.text: Purus meets the delivery-time requirement.
Vantex's first-year cost, before any credit, is below Finance's $30,000 limit.
If Vantex lowered its defect rate to 1.4 percent, its first-year cost would be lower than ClearPath's credited cost.

questions.explanation: Purus needs 12 business days, more than the 10 allowed: No. Vantex's first-year cost is 2,400 × 11.20 + 900 = 26,880 + 900 = $27,780, below $30,000: Yes. With a 1.4 percent defect rate Vantex would qualify, and $27,780 is below ClearPath's credited $29,066.80 (Vantex gets no credit): Yes.

tabs.title: Project charter
tabs.text: The CRM migration project has an approved budget of $480,000 for the fiscal year, divided into four categories: vendor licences, contractor fees, internal staff time and contingency. Contingency is 10 percent of the approved budget and may be spent only with the project sponsor's written approval. Any category whose total spending (actual plus forecast) exceeds its allocation by more than 15 percent must be reported to the steering committee.

tabs.title: Project manager's e-mail
tabs.text: The contractor overrun comes from a data-cleansing workstream that was not in the original plan. I propose to cover it from contingency. The sponsor has approved, in writing, the use of up to $30,000 of contingency for this purpose and nothing else.

questions.stem: By what percent is total spending on contractor fees expected to exceed the contractor fees allocation?
questions.explanation: Total contractor spending is 162,000 + 54,000 = $216,000 against an allocation of $180,000. The overrun is $36,000, and 36,000 ÷ 180,000 = 0.20, or 20 percent. Dividing the overrun by total spending instead (36,000 ÷ 216,000) gives only about 16.7 percent, and 36 percent mistakes the overrun in thousands of dollars for a percent.

questions.prompt: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true based on the information provided. Otherwise select No.

statements.text: The contractor fees category must be reported to the steering committee.
The approved contingency is enough, on its own, to cover the whole contractor overrun.
Internal staff time is expected to exceed its allocation.

questions.explanation: The 20 percent overrun is more than 15 percent, so it must be reported: Yes. The sponsor approved only $30,000 of contingency, less than the $36,000 overrun: No. Internal staff time totals 70,000 + 28,000 = $98,000, below its $102,000 allocation: No.

questions.stem: Suppose the $30,000 of approved contingency is applied to the contractor overrun and the expected underspend in internal staff time is also moved to contractor fees. How much of the contractor overrun would remain uncovered?
questions.explanation: The overrun is $36,000. Approved contingency covers $30,000, leaving $6,000. Internal staff time is expected to come in $4,000 under its allocation (102,000 - 98,000), which reduces the gap to 6,000 - 4,000 = $2,000. Choosing $6,000 forgets the staff-time underspend.

tabs.title: HR planning memo
tabs.text: Next year the company will grow its total headcount by 12 percent from the current 250 employees. At year end, Engineering must make up at least 40 percent of total headcount. Voluntary attrition is expected to equal 8 percent of each department's current headcount, and every departure will be backfilled with a new hire in addition to the planned net additions.

tabs.title: CFO e-mail
tabs.text: For budgeting, assume recruiting costs (agency fees and interview time) of $9,000 per Engineering hire and $5,000 per hire in every other department. Total recruiting cost for the year must stay below $500,000.

questions.stem: How many people in total will the company need to hire next year under the plan?
questions.explanation: Hires = backfills + net additions. Backfills are 8 percent of current headcount: 8 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 20 (8 percent of 250). Net additions total 30 (12 percent of 250). So the company hires 20 + 30 = 50 people. Choosing 30 counts only growth and ignores attrition.

questions.stem: If total net additions stay at 30, what is the smallest number of net additions in Engineering that satisfies the 40 percent requirement?
questions.explanation: Year-end headcount is 250 + 30 = 280, and 40 percent of 280 is 112. Engineering has 100 people now, and backfills only replace departures, so it needs at least 112 - 100 = 12 net additions. The planned 16 exceeds this minimum.

questions.prompt: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true based on the information provided. Otherwise select No.

statements.text: Total recruiting cost under the plan will be below the CFO's limit.
Recruiting cost for Engineering alone will be more than half of the CFO's limit.
If Sales' net additions rose by 12 and all other plans were unchanged, Engineering would still make up at least 40 percent of year-end headcount.

questions.explanation: Engineering hires = 8 + 16 = 24, costing 24 × 9,000 = $216,000; the other departments hire 26 people at $5,000, or $130,000. The total, $346,000, is below $500,000: Yes. $216,000 is less than half of $500,000 ($250,000): No. With 12 more Sales additions, year-end headcount is 292 and Engineering is 116; 116 ÷ 292 is about 39.7 percent, below 40 percent: No.

tabs.title: Event lead's e-mail
tabs.text: We are booking a venue for our two-day partner summit. Expected attendance is 180 people on day one and 140 on day two. The venue must (1) have a capacity at least 10 percent above the larger day's expected attendance, (2) be within 30 minutes of the airport and (3) provide on-site audio-visual (AV) equipment, either included or for an extra fee. Venue hire for both days, including any AV fee, must not exceed $16,000.

tabs.title: Finance reply
